reading.body:
Banking is where AI governance predates the AI boom by more than a decade: Fed SR 11-7 model risk rules already cover credit and AML models, and generative AI in service and compliance is the new supervised frontier.

The pattern is that banking's AI oversight is older than the current generative wave. Credit and AML models have operated under SR 11-7 since 2011, so the sector enters the generative era with pre-existing validation, documentation, and model risk requirements. Treasury's report frames the supervisory conversation, and the Evident AI Banking Index provides a public scoreboard across talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency.

For AI specifically, this means generative deployments in service and compliance inherit a governance burden that most other industries lack. A bank cannot launch a customer-facing chatbot or compliance assistant without treating it as a model under SR 11-7, which slows deployment but also reduces the chance of unmanaged failures. The data does not show scale. It contains no figures on compute demand or power consumption for banking AI, and no adoption rates or model sizes. Governance is the constraint the data documents, not infrastructure.

summary: Fraud detection and credit modelling are decades old; generative AI in service and compliance is the new supervised frontier.

analysis.body:
Measured adoption of AI in banking and insurance is substantial and rising. Per the Census Bureau, 41.0% of firms in Finance and insurance (NAICS 52) answered Yes to whether they used AI in the last two weeks, up from 36.5% in the prior period. The question was first asked in September 2023. That figure covers the whole finance and insurance sector rather than banking alone, and it measures recent use rather than depth of deployment.

What banks are actually doing with the technology is tracked most closely by Evident Insights, whose Evident AI Index benchmarks and tracks AI adoption across financial services and scores the world's largest banks across dozens of quantitative maturity metrics, including talent, innovation, leadership and transparency. Evident describes the index as the closest thing banking has to a public AI scoreboard, and says that since launching in January 2023 it has generated significant debate and wide press coverage. Evident also publishes a LATAM edition, where Nubank holds the number one ranking in the 2026 index, and an index for insurance. Its own commentary notes that several of the world's biggest banks have quietly become AI-powered behemoths while tech companies took the early attention, and that banks are racing to incorporate the technology into almost everything they do.

On the vendor and model side, this site's Financial Models section catalogues the 1000 most-downloaded open financial models on the Hugging Face Hub, with licence, downloads and release date, refreshed daily, drawn from the Hugging Face Hub public API and sorted by all-time downloads. The section tracks models tuned for financial text, with tag provenance stated. This is a catalogue of what is available rather than a measure of what banks have bought or deployed.

The regulatory posture is the distinctive feature of this sector. Credit and AML models operate under the Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 model risk management guidance, issued in 2011, which means banking is the sector where AI governance predates the AI boom by more than a decade. The letter is listed in the Fed's 2011 supervisory letters index. Separately, Treasury's report on AI in financial services, covering uses, opportunities and risks, frames the US supervisory conversation. The excerpt of the Treasury page in this dataset concerns OFAC sanctions on a gold smuggling and money laundering network rather than AI, so it supports only the general point that Treasury is active on financial crime and illicit finance risk.

The sources here do not report ROI figures for AI in banking, and no cost, revenue or efficiency numbers appear in the material. The evidence is about adoption measurement, benchmarking and supervision rather than returns. A reader deciding whether to deploy should take from this that adoption is already mainstream in the sector, that public benchmarking exists through the Evident AI Index, and that any model used in credit or AML decisions will sit inside a model risk management regime that has been in force since 2011. The open model catalogue is a starting point for build-versus-buy thinking, not a deployment record.

https://evidentinsights.com/.brief: Evident Insights describes itself as an intelligence platform that benchmarks and tracks AI adoption across financial services, offering data, research and benchmarking to leaders in the sector. It publishes the Evident AI Index, which it says has generated debate and press coverage since launching in January 2023, and notes that its CEO, Alexandra Mousavizadeh, is a regular commentator on global AI trends. The page promotes a 2026 edition of the index for banks, due in October, along with insurance and Latin America editions and an annual invitation-only symposium for senior AI leaders in finance. It also cites a newsletter with over 15,000 subscribers and references coverage suggesting banks are racing to adopt AI while tech hiring in finance grows more competitive.

https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-rel.brief: On International Anti-Corruption Day, Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned 28 individuals and businesses tied to a Zimbabwe-based gold smuggling and money-laundering network led by Kamlesh Pattni. The Treasury says the scheme bribed officials, used trusted supporters to conceal ownership, and built a global web of companies to hide illicit activity, depriving Zimbabwe’s citizens of resource benefits while enriching corrupt officials and criminals. Acting Under Secretary Bradley T. Smith noted that “Corruption respects no borders” and that the action demonstrates a whole-of-government approach and collaboration with allies. The Treasury’s move is carried out under Executive Order 13818, which targets serious human-rights abuse and corruption worldwide. International Anti-Corruption Day, observed annually on December 9 since the 2003 UNCAC, aims to raise awareness of anti-corruption initiatives; the United Nations lists 189 parties to the convention.

https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisi.brief: This page lists the Federal Reserve Board of Governors’ 2011 supervision and regulation letters. It notes that a lock icon or https indicates a secure .gov connection and advises “Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.” It also contains guidance on prior notices concerning dividend declarations by savings association subsidiaries of savings and loan holding companies.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/te.brief: The page catalogues the 1000 most-downloaded open financial models on the Hugging Face Hub, listing each model's licence, download count and release date, and states that the list is refreshed daily. It says the data comes from the Hugging Face Hub public API, sorted by all-time downloads, with every model linking to its own Hub page. The page reports that it was last verified on 2026-10-06 and gives a citation format crediting The World of AI. It also notes that searches cover the full text of every published page on the site, which it says is rebuilt daily from primary sources.
